# Smuggling Methods During Prohibition (1920–1933)

Bootleggers developed increasingly creative methods for hiding alcohol in vehicles as federal agents intensified enforcement. Here are the major techniques:

## Modified Compartments and False Panels

Smugglers built hidden compartments into cars—false floors, hollowed-out door panels, and spaces behind seats or dashboards. These "trap compartments" became so sophisticated that some were operated with levers or cables from the driver's seat, allowing the driver to shift the hiding spot or dump cargo if stopped.

## Oversized Fuel Tanks

One of the most common tricks was installing enlarged or secondary gas tanks. Whiskey could be stored in tanks that appeared to be ordinary fuel tanks, or in dual-tank setups where one held gasoline and the other held liquor. Agents eventually learned to smell for alcohol or tap tanks to hear liquid levels.

## Concealment in Ordinary Parts

Liquor was hidden in:
- Hollowed-out spare tires
- Bumpers and running boards
- Under the hood in modified engine compartments
- Inside door frames and roof linings

## The "Cut-Down" and Speed Culture

Bootleggers famously modified cars for performance—souping up engines to outrun agents on rural roads. These modified vehicles later inspired stock car racing, and many early NASCAR drivers and mechanics got their start running moonshine.

## Trucks and False Loads

For larger shipments, smugglers used trucks carrying seemingly legitimate cargo—lumber, produce, or livestock—with alcohol concealed beneath or inside. Some used hearses, since agents were reluctant to search them.

## Escalating Cat-and-Mouse

As agents caught on, both sides escalated: customs officers used X-ray equipment and probes, while smugglers responded with more elaborate compartments and faster cars. This arms race made smuggling a genuinely technical trade during the Prohibition years.
